{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=preference+formation+memory+dependent+decisions+path+dependence+longitudinal+behavior+active+learning&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Closing the Loop on the Cocktail Party Effect: From Attention Decoding to Neuro-Steered Selective Hearing.\", \"abstract\": \"Selective hearing in multi-talker environments remains a central challenge for assistive listening technologies: conventional devices improve audibility but cannot infer which talker the listener intends to follow. This Perspective examines the emerging transition from auditory attention decoding to neuro-steered selective hearing. We argue that a recent real-time intracranial proof-of-principle study marks an important inflection point in this transition, because it shows, under high-fidelity recordings from neurosurgical patients and in controlled two-talker conditions, that decoded neural attention can be coupled online to relative-gain control, thereby improving speech perception and reducing listening effort within that experimental setting. Building on this proof of principle, we argue that the field should move beyond offline decoding accuracy as its primary benchmark and instead treat neuro-steered hearing as a closed-loop translational problem linking neural inference, acoustic scene analysis, and control policy. From this perspective, future benchmarks should integrate device-level control metrics, including latency, effective switch time, false-switch rate and recovery after erroneous updates, with listener-centered outcomes such as speech intelligibility, listening effort, user preference and everyday benefit. Accordingly, we outline a staged roadmap for electroencephalography-based systems, from controlled two-speaker paradigms to scene-aware control and ultimately wearable real-world implementations. We also discuss the complementary roles of magnetoencephalography, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, and functional magnetic resonance imaging in defining the neural mechanisms and design constraints of future systems. {"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=meta-reasoning+architectures+autonomous+foundational+revision+epistemic+assumptions&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Generative AI for Personalized Learning Platforms in Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Education: Scoping Review.\", \"abstract\": \"

Background

Generative AI, including large language models (LLMs), may enable personalized learning in medical education. In otolaryngology-head and neck surgery (ear, nose, and throat [ENT]) education, AI may support knowledge retrieval, adaptive assessment, feedback, and scalable learning, but evidence remains fragmented.

Objective

This scoping review aimed to map generative AI research in otolaryngology education; summarize applications, performance, benefits, and risks; and identify directions for AI-enabled personalized learning.

Methods

We included English-language empirical studies, preprints, and technical or developmental evaluations published from 2017 through 2026 with direct relevance to professional ENT education; nonempirical publications and studies without a professional educational focus were excluded. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, and CINAHL were searched, supplemented by citation searching. The final search was conducted on July 6, 2026. Data were charted using a standardized form by 2 reviewers and synthesized through a 3-stage inductive thematic analysis, with third reviewer adjudication. No formal critical appraisal or meta-analysis was performed because of study heterogeneity.

Results

A total of 42 studies published between 2023 and 2026 were included. Most were performance studies (n=33, 78.6%), followed by system development (n=3, 7.1%), educational intervention studies (n=3, 7.1%), surveys (n=2, 4.8%), and guideline development (n=1, 2.4%). Most studies evaluated question sets or model outputs rather than participants. Applications included knowledge retrieval, revision, board-style question practice, adaptive assessment, AI avatar-delivered instruction, and operative-planning support.
